claims.text: Applying a thin, conformal Ti/Ni or similar refractory-metal coating to tungsten surfaces before consolidation will suppress phase separation in W–Cu composites.
The interfacial coating will suppress void formation at W/Cu interfaces.
The coating will improve the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites under high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites containing tungsten particles or interconnected ligaments in copper display phase separation during processing and service.
Untreated W–Cu composites develop voids at the W/Cu interface during processing and service.
A coating can mediate interface structure and enhance bonding or compatibility between a particle and its matrix.
The proposed Ti/Ni coating will act as a diffusion barrier at the W/Cu interface.
Inhibiting interdiffusion at the W/Cu interface will inhibit void nucleation during thermal and irradiation exposure.
The coating will reduce W/Cu interfacial energy.
A tailored interlayer will limit deleterious atomic interactions at the W/Cu interface and thereby prevent phase separation.
Interface stabilization will minimize void formation and preserve continuous heat-conduction pathways.
Coated W–Cu composites will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than untreated controls after identical high-heat-flux and irradiation exposures.
Reduced interfacial defects and enhanced bonding are the causes of the predicted thermal-conductivity improvement.
Pronounced interfacial voids in untreated W–Cu composites cause inferior thermal conductivity.
The intervention is expected to remain effective under processing and service environments representative of plasma-facing W/Cu joints.
The coating may lose efficacy if it degrades at extremely high temperatures or under prolonged irradiation.
The optimal coating thickness and its long-term stability under extreme service conditions remain undetermined.
The quantitative thermal-conductivity improvement requires empirical validation.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies an 'optimized Ti/Ni layer,' while the uncertainty field states that the precise optimal thickness remains to be determined.
